text:
Citation:

R. v. Koopman

2024 BCPC 210

Date:

20241003

File Nos:

AJ6525763-1

AJ6525763-6

Registry:

Chilliwack

IN THE
PROVINCIAL COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

REX

v.

JOHN KOOPMAN

ORAL RULING

OF THE

HONOURABLE JUDGE
A. ORMISTON

Counsel for the Crown:

M. B. Rankin, K.C. and
D.J. Williams

Counsel for the Defendant:

P.E. Jaffe
and
M. Moore

Places of Hearing:

Abbotsford
and Chilliwack, B.C.

Dates of Hearing:

January 21, August
11-12, 15-16, 2022, March 7-9, May 15-18
December 6, 2023, April 12, July 22, 2024

Date
of Judgment:

October 3, 2024

[
1
]

THE COURT:   This decision relates to Ticket
Number AJ06525763. Pastor John Koopman brings an application to judicially stay
violation tickets issued to him in December of 2020, based on alleged abuse of
process. He has been found guilty of hosting in‑person events that were
prohibited in the early days of the COVID‑19 pandemic. The tickets issued
to Pastor Koopman are four of 19 that have been before this Court since the
spring of 2021. Findings of guilt have been made on all tickets; however,
convictions have been held in abeyance pending resolution of constitutional
challenges brought by the defendants.

[
2
]

On agreement of counsel, the Court has heard
various applications in relation to Pastor Koopman's ticket as the ‘lead
ticket,’ in order to efficiently settle identical legal issues that have been
raised on all 19 tickets.

Overview of the Litigation

[
3
]

From beginning to end of this litigation, Pastor
Koopman and the other defendants have maintained the position that their rights
to freely practice religion have been unfairly fettered by the state and, in
particular, by orders made by the Provincial Health Officer (‘the PHO’). While
this argument has been pursued down different legal pathways I feel confident
now, having heard directly from the defendants, in saying that the central
concern that brings these men before the Court is their passionate and earnest
belief that unfair, immoral, and illegal restrictions were placed on their
ability to gather for worship. In the course of this latest hearing it has
become clear that the engine driving this applicant, Pastor Koopman, into
conflict with the law is that he does not believe the state can forbid people
to gather for worship.

[
4
]

Pastor Koopman is not a so‑called COVID
denier. He has found this conflict between his faith and the law to be
exquisitely painful. Pastor Koopman personally, and his church generally, took
the COVID restrictions seriously in the initial months following the
declaration of a state of emergency in 2020. But ultimately, when the PHO
decided restrictions would no longer be sufficient and a prohibition on in‑person
worship services was required, Pastor Koopman disagreed. He did not believe
that the reconsideration process that was in place to provide exemptions to the
prohibition on gathering would be responsive to his dilemma, in part because he
had been trying without success to impress upon the PHO the importance of in‑person
worship in the months leading up to the prohibitions.

[
5
]

Pastor Koopman and several of the other
defendants in this litigation pursued a judicial review in order to advance the
argument that the PHO's gathering and events orders were unconstitutional. That
case,
Beaudoin v. British Columbia
, was heard by the Supreme Court,
2021
BCSC 512
, and upheld by our Court of Appeal,
2022 BCCA 427
. In
Beaudoin
,
the Court reviewed the decision making of the PHO. This bears repeating here
today, given the singular focus of the individuals who testified before me
about the sanctity of their constitutional rights under
ss. 2
,
7
, and
15
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

[
6
]

I have had the benefit of hearing first‑hand
from these witnesses, including Pastor Koopman, given the Crown's willingness
to allow much of their testimony into evidence, despite its arguable legal
inadmissibility. I have heard the applicant and others explain why they
violated the gathering and events orders. I accept the intensity of their moral
dilemma. I accept their evidence about the suffering they felt personally and
on behalf of their congregations during the COVID restrictions. And I accept
that if they had followed the orders, it would have caused them hardship that
is not at all trivial. I have heard why they believe that the PHO had no basis
and no right to make the orders that she did.

[
7
]

However, the decision that I have to make today
is not a moral or religious one, that is clearly not my role. My decision is a
legal one and it is determined by the fact that the gathering and events orders
have been found by the courts in
Beaudoin
to be justified breaches of
the right to gather for religious worship. In other words, the government
interference in religious matters, to which several of the witnesses in this
hearing have objected, has already been found to be a legitimate, rational, and
fair balancing of important freedoms with the need to stop preventable deaths
from occurring and to preserve the capacity of our healthcare system.

[
8
]

Despite the somewhat surprising evidence of at
least one witness for the applicant, let me make clear that our Court of Appeal
in
Beaudoin
definitively and thoroughly decided the issue of whether
these temporary infringements on religious freedoms were a proportionate
response to the public health emergency in the early days of the COVID‑19
pandemic. This was the defining issue decided in
Beaudoin
.

[
9
]

The Court in
Beaudoin
also dealt with
questions many of the witnesses in this hearing have found so vexatious, such
as why people could go to grocery stores, to the gym, to a hockey game, or
support groups, but not gather in person to worship. The answer that is fleshed
out in
Beaudoin
is that different gatherings can have different risks
when it comes to the spread of disease, given variables like the nature of the
contact between people, how long they are there, the activities they perform (including
whether they sing or touch each other or stay in close proximity for extended
periods), who is present, in particular their age and vulnerability to
infection. These are all factors that impact risk. Notably not among the risk
factors is whether the activities are secular or religious.

[
10
]

The judicial review of the PHO's decision
making, where Chief Justice Hinkson found an ample evidentiary basis for the
PHO to reasonably conclude that when people gathered for worship the factors I
mentioned above created a risk of COVID transmission that was unacceptably high,
stands in stark contrast to counsel's characterization of the PHO's decisions
as "patently nutty".

[
11
]

Moreover, the evidence during this litigation
has answered the defendant's own question about why meetings like support
groups have different risks than worship gatherings. Some witnesses have
described worship services occurring every Sunday throughout the early pandemic
when events were prohibited, for sustained periods of time, in large numbers,
indoors, with singing, speaking, and sometimes without masks.

[
12
]

There is absolutely no foundation to say, as
applicant's counsel repeatedly has, that the PHO prohibited worship simply
because it was worship. Worship itself was not prohibited at all. Gatherings
and events were prohibited. Worship services are one of many forms of
gathering. Baptisms, weddings, funerals were permitted with certain
restrictions, and exemptions could be sought to the prohibition on gathering
and events. Exemptions were granted for worship services where there was a plan
to follow increased restrictions to mitigate the risk of infection spreading.

[
13
]

I take the time to review this history in part
because counsel for Pastor Koopman insisted at the screening hearing that this
abuse of process application was not simply an attempt to relitigate the issues
that have been already decided in
Beaudoin
. This Court was clear at the
Haevischer

hearing that the precedent set in
Beaudoin
would not and could not be
revisited at this hearing. Nevertheless, counsel has made submissions urging
this Court to do just that. Specifically, counsel maintains that the evidence
heard on the abuse of process hearing is such that this Court should consider
itself not to be bound by
stare decisis
, and to consider anew the
constitutional questions that were answered in
Beaudoin
.

Revisiting
Beaudoin

[
14
]

I am going to begin by addressing this argument about the binding
nature of the ruling in
Beaudoin
, because the majority of evidence led
on this hearing focused on allegations that the gathering and events orders
were, as I have said, unfair, immoral, or illegal curtailments of our religious
freedoms. Leaving aside the procedural issues around counsel disregarding my
Haevischer

ruling or ambushing the respondent with this argument, there is no merit to the
submission that this Court should reopen the constitutional questions that were
closed in
Beaudoin
.

[
15
]

Applicant's counsel continues to suggest that
Beaudoin

is wrong and unfair, despite having been fully and finally settled all the way
through to the Supreme Court of Canada refusing to hear an appeal of our Court
of Appeal's unanimous decision. The applicant also seeks, again, to distinguish

Beaudoin
, much as they did in their original applications alleging

s. 2
,
7
, and
15

Charter
breaches, submitting that facts established
at this hearing that were not part of the record in
Beaudoin
require
revisiting that decision. He further submits the PHO acted in bad faith and
dishonestly in ways that would make it unjust to follow the precedent set in
Beaudoin
.

[
16
]

The applicable law regarding the binding nature
of constitutional decisions is found in
Bedford v. Canada
,
2013 SCC 72
,
and it has been relied upon by higher courts in a similar context of challenges
more recently.
Beaudoin
itself was recently decided and was not resolved
in favour of the petitioners, despite much of the evidence mirroring what is
now before this Court. While some of the evidence here did not inform the
decision in
Beaudoin
, such as excerpts from Dr. Henry's book and
some correspondence relating to the reconsideration process, none of what is
now before me invalidates the precedent set in
Beaudoin
. I will explain
the reasons for this finding in a moment when I go through the factual basis
for the abuse of process application itself, because both arguments rely on the
same allegations of fact interwoven throughout the applicant's submissions.

[
17
]

At the heart of the applicant's submission that
the precedent in
Beaudoin
should not be binding is the contention that
through deceit and bad faith, the PHO and/or the government manufactured the
outcome of the case in
Beaudoin
and stripped the defendants of their
ability to challenge the gathering and events orders. These allegations are
rooted in the same factual basis alleged on the abuse of process claim, and I
will go through my factual findings momentarily.

[
18
]

My conclusion is that the alleged state
misconduct has not been established. What has been proven falls far short of
the kind of new evidence, fraud, or injustice that would be required for this
Court to depart from the precedent established in
Beaudoin
.

Legal Framework for an Abuse of
Process

[
19
]

Before I review the factual basis for the
present application, I will address the legal framework in which this abuse of
process application has been brought. The applicant asserts violations of his
Charter

rights under
ss. 7
and
11(d)
. These are provisions that protect life, liberty,
security of the person, and an accused's rights to a fair trial. The applicant
has said almost nothing about how they have met the requisite burden under
these sections.

[
20
]

I agree with Crown counsel that an application
under
s. 7
fails on the threshold issue that life, liberty, and security
of the person are not engaged, given that the prosecution will result, at most,
in a fine: see
R. v. Blencoe
at paragraph 55 and
R. v. Richard
at
paragraph 8. Even if this threshold issue were met, the applicant has not
established a
s. 7
breach that is independent of the
s. 2
breach that
has already been found to be justified in
Beaudoin
.

[
21
]

Much of the applicant's s. 11(d) argument
has already been summarily dismissed. A significant part of this argument
alleges prosecutorial misconduct in the course of the
Beaudoin

proceedings. As I found at the
Haevischer
application, and still find
now, there is no basis to advance such a claim. The applicant has not made
clear how exactly the s. 11(d) action is otherwise engaged when the
offences Pastor Koopman committed predate much of the conduct that is said to
be an abuse of process.

[
22
]

Finally, the applicant relies on common law
doctrines of abuse of process. He submits that the PHO's conduct in making the orders
and administering the reconsideration regime was exercised in such bad faith
that this Court should refuse to enter a conviction again Pastor Koopman
because of the need for the justice system to distance itself from egregiously
bad conduct by a public officer.

[
23
]

While the legal basis for this application is
not necessarily clear or straightforward, the determinative issues are factual.
Both the
Charter
and the common law arguments alike rely on asserted
facts regarding conduct of the PHO that I ultimately find have not been
established. Given the ways in which the scope of this hearing was narrowed
following the Crown's screening application, the primary factual issue is
whether the regime allowing the PHO to grant exceptions to prohibitions on
gathering and events was administered in bad faith.

[
24
]

It is important to make clear, given the tenor
of submissions made by counsel, that it is not an absence of expert or other
opinion evidence that leads these claims to fail. These claims have failed on
the basis of factual evidence that has been tendered. Based on the evidence led
in this hearing, I find no merit or reason behind the conspiratorial theories
about a web of dishonesty and malevolence directed towards the applicant and
the other defendants. I will go through these factual issues now.

Factual
Foundation

[
25
]

The applicant makes several representations regarding how the PHO
administered the reconsideration regime under s. 43 of the
Public
Health Act
. Any suggestion that this regime failed this particular applicant,
Pastor Koopman, can be swiftly rejected. He did not make a reconsideration
request until well after violating the orders, and when he did, he received an
exemption in short order. He did not seek the exemptions that other religious
leaders were granted, and when they were extended to him, he continued to
violate the orders.

[
26
]

However, the applicant makes arguments at this
hearing that go beyond his own experience with the s. 43 reconsideration
process. He alleges broader systemic conduct in an attempt to show that the
entire s. 43 regime was, at best, ineffective and, at worst, a deceptive
sham. He not only marshals this evidence to explain his own lack of engagement
with the process, he ultimately submits that the state misconduct requires a
stay of proceedings because it is so egregious that to enter convictions
against him or the other defendants would undermine the integrity of the
judicial process.

[
27
]

The primary factual assertions made by the
applicant about the reconsideration process are that: (1) the PHO ignored
requests for reconsideration; (2) the PHO applied the s. 43 process
unfairly and inconsistently; and finally (3) this conduct rendered the s. 43
process itself a sham, and the PHO and others knew it, which they intentionally
hid from the Court in
Beaudoin
.

Did the PHO Ignore Requests for
Reconsideration?

[
28
]

At the screening hearing, the applicant asserted
that this Court would hear evidence that hundreds of thousands of citizens
requested reconsideration and were ignored by the PHO. This evidence did not
materialize.

[
29
]

What the applicant did establish is that some
people and organizations wrote to the PHO and did not receive a response. The
PHO was entitled under the legislation not to respond and this makes sense,
given her role in managing a public health emergency. The nature of the
unanswered correspondence is important to consider, given the inference the
applicant invites the Court to make: that the PHO was routinely acting with an
"arrogant disregard" for the rights of citizens, in particular people
concerned about their ability to worship.

[
30
]

Most of the requests that were submitted by
religious leaders on behalf of congregations, which counsel submits represents
thousands of people in total, questioned whether the PHO had struck the right
balance in weighing their right to gather in person for worship against her
public health objectives. They asked for recision of the orders, not specific
exemptions.  They were not responsive to the PHO's conclusion that something
more than the restrictions that had previously been in place would be required.

[
31
]

Many of the examples marshaled by the applicant did involve a
response of some kind from the PHO's office, even if it was a ‘form letter.’
This does not support the argument that the requests for reconsideration were
simply being ignored, especially given the nature of many of the requests
themselves, which were essentially requests to rescind the prohibition and
return to restrictions. It was an efficient way to advise applicants that their
request could not be granted.

[
32
]

From the evidence led at the hearing, it appears
that churches were also using a form letter of sorts to send to the PHO to
ensure that their principled objections to the prohibitions were heard.
Applicant's counsel attempts to characterize this as proof that thousands of
people were being ignored in the reconsideration process. This is not a fair
interpretation of the correspondence. While religious leaders submitted letters
on behalf of their congregations and Mr. Sikkema asked for reconsideration
on behalf of multiple different churches, this is not the same thing as saying
the PHO was routinely ignoring thousands of requests for reconsideration.

[
33
]

What makes this particular abuse of process allegation so weak is
the fact that even when the PHO did not respond directly to some of the
requests for exemptions for a whole class of people, such as for entire
congregations, variances that the PHO made to the prohibition on gathering in
the months after these letters were sent strongly suggests that she was responsive
to the concerns raised by the precise people applicant's counsel submits were
being ignored. The variances may not have been precisely what was being sought,
but it is untenable to say that this class of people, with concerns about being
unable to gather for in‑person worship, were simply being ignored.

[
34
]

The evidence before me does not establish a
systemic failure in the reconsideration process that would constitute an abuse
of process or give this Court any basis to interfere with the binding authority
in
Beaudoin
.

Did the PHO Apply the Reconsideration
Regime Unfairly?

[
35
]

Applicant's counsel went beyond submitting that
the PHO was ignoring reconsideration requests generally, which was an issue
dealt with to some extent in
Beaudoin
. The applicant here also submits
that the PHO was ignoring certain classes of reconsideration requests, namely
those submitted by religious groups generally, and Christians specifically.
This argument took several different forms, from suggesting that the religious
petitioners in
Beaudoin
were being unfairly penalized for speaking up
against the PHO's orders, to submitting preferential treatment was being given
to certain denominations who were successful in their reconsideration requests.

[
36
]

There is no basis in the evidence to find that
the applicant specifically, or Christian churches generally, were targeted in
this way. Counsel for the applicant argues that the PHO's form letter
responses, late responses, or in some cases no direct responses to religious
leaders demonstrate a cavalier attitude about the impact of the prohibitions on
constitutionally‑protected rights, including the right to freely gather
and practice one's religion. However, this position is not supported by the
evidence or the law.

[
37
]

First, the findings of the Court in
Beaudoin
regarding the PHO's approach to competing rights was that the PHO
appropriately balanced her mandates regarding public health with the
constitutionally‑protected rights of Canadians.

[
38
]

Second, as I have said already, the PHO may not
have always responded directly to specific requests by religious leaders to
rescind the prohibition, but the variances she made in March of 2021
specifically for worship services were responsive to their concerns.

[
39
]

Third, there is evidence that the PHO convened
meetings with faith leaders to discuss issues around prohibitions, even if they
were limited.

[
40
]

Fourth, the office of the PHO demonstrated a
willingness to meet the needs of religious people: for example, when the Deputy
PHO granted exemptions for limited in‑person worship to rabbis of
orthodox Jewish synagogues.

[
41
]

Finally, and most significantly, the PHO wrote directly to the
applicant on December 18, 2020, personally inviting him to make a case‑specific
request for reconsideration. She referenced the fact that she had already
considered and granted these types of requests. This was not the first time the
PHO communicated directly with Pastor Koopman. This evidence strongly
contradicts the applicant's argument that the PHO was looking to sweep aside
religious freedoms. This correspondence completely undermines the broad
accusations that the PHO acted with an arrogant disregard towards Christians
generally, or Pastor Koopman specifically.

[
42
]

It is nothing short of remarkable, in my view,
that at the time, in the crush of a global health emergency of December 2020,
the PHO wrote directly to Pastor Koopman and invited him to make a
reconsideration request that gave her something to work with. One might think
the PHO would be entitled to simply ignore correspondence that states her
decisions were wrong and her orders would be disobeyed. Not only did the PHO
not ignore Pastor Koopman's legitimate concerns about how he would exercise his
faith in these times and support others in doing the same, she wrote him to
tell him what she needed from him to be able to do something that could help.

[
43
]

In my view, this evidence points to the exact opposite inference
that the applicant wants the Court to draw. In other words, this correspondence
does not suggest that the PHO treated the applicant and similarly concerned
church leaders with arrogant disregard. She appears to have treated them as
people deserving of special standing.

[
44
]

I have not been pointed to any rational reason
why the PHO's overtures to Pastor Koopman should be interpreted as anything
other than an earnest attempt to reach some kind of solution where people could
gather to worship, while public health objectives could also be maintained.

[
45
]

Pastor Koopman was, as he has been throughout
these proceedings, candid in saying that perhaps he could have responded to the
PHO's letter differently. He was understandably frustrated by watching the
suffering within his congregation and community, given the restrictions that
were already in place. He was truly devastated by the news of the prohibitions
and feeling helpless, given that in the months leading up to the prohibitions
there was no consultation, or ‘direct line,’ so to speak, to the people in
power who were making the decisions.

[
46
]

I do not doubt that the burden on Pastor Koopman
as he tried to advocate for his congregation was heavy, but I am satisfied that
these hardships were not caused by bad faith, malice, or deception by the PHO.
Her conduct may not have been perfect either, but it falls far short of bad
faith or an abuse of process.

[
47
]

I can find no merit or reason in any of
counsel's submissions regarding how the petitioners in
Beaudoin
were
somehow targeted or penalized by the PHO. In general terms, counsel's
assertions about the
Beaudoin
proceedings do not take into account legal
realities and the consequences that flowed from the decisions made by the
applicant and other petitioners.

[
48
]

Counsel also advances the argument that some
religious groups were receiving preferential treatment because their requests
for reconsideration were answered and granted by the office of the PHO, while
the applicant and other representatives for Christian churches were not.

[
49
]

This argument that preferential or biased
decisions were made in relation to synagogues who requested the exemptions has
no merit. The email correspondence on which these exemptions were based makes
clear that Rabbi Kaplan made a different request than the ones made in the letters
tendered here from the churches. Rabbi Kaplan requested a time‑limited
exemption and he agreed to abide by restrictions that went beyond the ones that
were in place before the prohibitions were imposed. Namely, he agreed to gather
in smaller numbers outdoors, with the assurance that no one would come within
six feet of another person other than their family.  Assurance was also given
that masks would be worn by everyone for the entire service.

[
50
]

Some of the requests by the churches made proposals for safety
measures, but not ones that answered the specific concerns the PHO had
identified about large indoor gatherings where participants sing. The requests
that applicant’s counsel submits were ignored were not responsive to the fact
that the PHO had determined previous measures like masking, contact tracing,
cleaning, and social distancing, were no longer going to be sufficient on their
own. Some correspondence promised to disobey the orders if the prohibitions
were not immediately rescinded.

[
51
]

Counsel spent a great deal of time emphasizing
the casual nature of the correspondence between Rabbi Kaplan and the Deputy
PHO. His submission that the church requests were being unfairly rejected
because they were not in the proper form makes no sense, because it overlooks
the glaringly obvious difference between the substance of the requests that
were being made by the different faith groups.

[
52
]

The evidence tendered at this hearing does not
even come close to establishing that the PHO granted the rabbi's reconsideration
request based on any kind of bias or preferential treatment. Different
decisions were made on the basis of different requests.

[
53
]

Counsel's suggestion that Dr. Emerson told Rabbi Kaplan worship
services were low risk, while Dr. Henry told the
Beaudoin
petitioners
that worship services were high risk is not an accurate or fair interpretation
of the correspondence. Dr. Emerson's November 27, 2020, letter states he
is satisfied that the plan and circumstances proposed by Rabbi Kaplan would
make their gathering low risk. This was a plan that was not proposed by the
applicant. Dr. Henry's
reference to elevated risk in her letter to Pastor Koopman must be read in the
context of trying to address his concerns that the risks from the COVID
pandemic did not warrant the strict limitation of religious freedoms.

[
54
]

Counsel for the applicant goes on to argue the
PHO should be found to have acted in bad faith because in making the gathering
and events orders so broad, she failed to apply the least‑restrictive
measures in order to meet her public health objectives. If she could allow one
faith group to gather for worship outside, why prohibit the others entirely?

[
55
]

Assuming the PHO could be found to have acted in
bad faith by failing to apply the least restrictive measures, which is arguable
in and of itself, and inconsistent with the s. 1 analysis in
Beaudoin
,
the submission itself is illogical and not at all persuasive. Essentially, it
is submitted that because the PHO was prepared to grant a reconsideration
request to Rabbi Kaplan, she had a duty to extend the same exemption to all
religious groups.

[
56
]

By its very nature, the process for
reconsideration was going to result in difference. It was, after all, a process
for granting exceptions to the rule that would allow flexibility and mitigate
the ways in which necessary public health orders would interfere with the
exercise of important civil rights. This does not necessarily mean it would
always be safe to grant the same exemptions to everyone, regardless of whether
they asked for them or not, and regardless of whether they had an adequate plan
or intended to follow them. If
this were the case, the prohibition itself could just be varied.

[
57
]

Indeed, the PHO did vary the prohibition on
gathering for all worship services by March of 2021. None of the Christian
churches I heard about at this hearing asked for the same exceptions being
sought by Rabbi Kaplan, nor did they want them, given that they continued to
gather, some in very large numbers, indoors in contravention of both the
original prohibition and the subsequent variance.

[
58
]

The closest the evidence in this case comes to
discrepant treatment is the fact that for a period of four days in February
2021, the Deputy PHO granted a class exemption for orthodox Jewish synagogues
to conduct worship services indoors, while the petitioners in the
Beaudoin

proceeding were only granted an exemption to worship outdoors. This was corrected
by the PHO who quickly clarified that the synagogues had only ever been granted
permission to worship indoors for a specific holiday, and they would also have
to return to gathering outdoors, just like the petitioners in
Beaudoin
.

[
59
]

Applicant's counsel submits this apparent
difference in the PHO's responses reveals that her decision making was
ungoverned by science or any legitimate public health objective. They want the
Court to draw the inference that the PHO only made the exemption for both faith
groups consistent because she had been caught allowing an exemption that she
was unfairly withholding from the applicant and others. This allegation defies
belief, particularly given the broader factual context.

[
60
]

First, the full record of the email correspondence
suggests that the request to worship indoors was only for the holiday of Purim
and the following sabbath, not for ongoing weekly worship services. While the
Deputy PHO's response leaves room for confusion about whether he granted an
ongoing or time‑limited exemption, the PHO's subsequent message clarifies
that the request and the exemption granted were both limited to one particular
holiday.

[
61
]

Even if there were a genuine difference in the
exemption granted by the PHO and her Deputy, it was extremely short lived and
not consistent with the nefarious motives the applicant seeks to impute to the
PHO. The inferences the applicant urges the Court to draw are not compatible
with other reliable evidence. The applicant's position rests on the Court
accepting the PHO wanted to hide the difference in these reconsideration
decisions from the applicant and from the public.

[
62
]

However, the PHO herself told Pastor Koopman that she had granted
reconsideration requests for others in her December letter. There was further
information about these reconsideration decisions contained in Dr. Emerson's
affidavit disclosed to the petitioners in the
Beaudoin
proceedings.
These facts are inconsistent with the conclusion that the PHO was attempting to
obfuscate exemptions that she had made for others.

[
63
]

The applicant's submissions regarding the dark
secrecy of the PHO and the government are made as if the
Public Health Act

did not exist and the PHO was free to tread on the privacy rights of those who
wrote to her asking for a reconsideration. It makes sense that the PHO could
only release correspondence her office had with the rabbis pursuant to a court
order.

[
64
]

On the basis of the broader evidence about
requests for reconsideration by different faith groups, I have no difficulty
rejecting the assertion that the PHO was giving preferential treatment to any
one faith group over the other in her requests for reconsideration. It is an
illogical leap to assume, from the limited exemption given to one group and not
the other, that there was a deep‑seated bias and prejudice working
against the applicant.

[
65
]

Applicant's counsel argues they are entitled to the most favourable
interpretation of the evidence arising from this email correspondence, given
that no one from the PHO's office testified to explain the messages. Even if I were to accept that there was an
irregularity, mistake, or miscommunication when the Deputy PHO granted the
indoor exemption to the synagogues, the correction made by the PHO days later
does not suggest the kind of bad faith that constitutes an abuse of process. In
fact, it suggests quite the opposite.

Did the PHO Mislead the Court about the
Reconsideration Regime?

[
66
]

The final aspect of the applicant's argument
regarding the s. 43 regime is that the PHO and other state actors are
alleged to have misled the Court in
Beaudoin
and, as such, I should find
that the constitutional decisions made in that case were achieved through fraud
and deception.

[
67
]

This argument is also doomed to fail. First, the
applicant's counsel has resurrected allegations of injustice, dishonesty, and
malice by counsel and, to some extent, the Court in
Beaudoin
for
accepting a distorted record on which to decide the constitutional issues at
hand. I have already dismissed allegations of prosecutorial misconduct and
collateral attacks on the
Beaudoin
decision. The adequacy of the record
on which Court made its decision in
Beaudoin
is certainly not for me to
decide.

[
68
]

While it may be open to this Court to reconsider constitutional
decisions where they are built on fraud or dishonesty, there is no such thing
established here. The applicant alleges the PHO never intended to respond to
requests for reconsideration in good faith, or that she was not able to respond
to reconsideration requests but put forward in
Beaudoin
that the
reconsideration process was sound.

[
69
]

The applicant has not established that the
reconsideration regime was broken. The factual circumstances I have already
outlined contradict that assertion. Most of the evidence marshalled here has
already been considered by the Court in
Beaudoin
. The additional
evidence led in this hearing that some people did not receive direct responses,
or did not receive the responses they wanted, is incapable of supporting the
conclusion that the system was broken or a sham.

[
70
]

The applicant relies heavily on the experience
of Pastor Vanderveen in submitting that the reconsideration regime was broken,
and that the PHO knew it when
Beaudoin
was argued. Pastor Vanderveen
wrote to the PHO with a request for reconsideration on December 7, 2020, and
again on January 7, 2021. He did not receive a reply until May 5, 2021, when
the Deputy PHO advised him that his request would no longer be reviewed because
it had become beyond the PHO’s capacity to manage.

[
71
]

Applicant's counsel submits this correspondence shows that the
reconsideration process had been completely overwhelmed and was unable to be
meaningfully implemented in back in December of 2020. However, Dr. Emerson's
email does not say that the system had completely shut down in late 2020. It
was in April of 2021 that the reconsideration process was suspended so the PHO
could better allocate her resources. The body of evidence I have already reviewed,
including the correspondence sent to this applicant in December 2020, supports
the finding that the PHO was engaging in the reconsideration process. Furthermore, in March 2021 variances to the
prohibition on gathering for in‑person worship were made that were
responsive to Pastor Vanderveen’s request.

[
72
]

In conclusion, there are not many instances
presented to this Court where the PHO failed to respond entirely to people
seeking exemptions. While this unfortunately did occur, it is not anywhere near
a degree that would suggest the system was inoperative. Not only was the Court
in
Beaudoin
aware that the PHO had not responded in a timely way to
Pastor Vanderveen when they rejected the applicant's claims about the efficacy
of the reconsideration process, but the Court of Appeal was also aware that the
reconsideration process had been suspended in April 2021.

[
73
]

The PHO's inaction must be fairly considered in terms of what is
reasonable to expect of a public official, especially this public official at
that time. The body of evidence
falls short of establishing the assertions of counsel that the PHO was
operating in bad faith or that she knowingly misled the Court about the
operation of the s. 43 regime.

Are there Other Reasons to Revisit
Beaudoin?

[
74
]

In addition to allegations that the PHO misled
the Court in
Beaudoin
about the integrity of the s. 43 process, the
applicant argues that the ruling should be revisited because there is new
evidence to consider, and because basic fairness dictates that the ruling in
Beaudoin

should not be binding.

[
75
]

Some of these arguments are collateral attacks,
given that counsel simply revisits matters that were raised and rejected when I
summarily dismissed the initial
Charter
application. For example,
allegations that excerpts from Dr. Henry's book show her decision making
was overthrown by political influence or untethered to her stated scientific
objectives. Applicant's counsel also argues that data about COVID cases led in this
hearing proves the PHO made decisions that were unsupported by scientific
evidence.

[
76
]

The applicant submits Mr. Roy’s data from B.C.C.D.C. shows the PHO's
decision making was in fact unreasonable. This is not an abuse of process
argument. This is a clear collateral attack on the decision in
Beaudoin
.
The Court of Appeal in
Beaudoin
considered whether to admit Mr. Roy's
evidence in deciding the constitutional validity of the PHO's decision making
and found it would not be helpful, because the raw numbers do not allow for an
adequate comparison of infection risk between different settings. This includes
data like how many people are present, how long they spend there, their
susceptibility to serious illness, and the nature of their interactions. The
data collected by Mr. Roy was a mere jumping‑off point to the more
detailed data examined by the PHO in order to assess risk.

[
77
]

Finally, the applicant asserts that the data
relied on at the time of the gathering and events orders was wrong by
overwhelming margins. This does nothing to advance the abuse of process
argument, nor does it invalidate the Court's findings in
Beaudoin
. The
constitutionality of the orders was based on what the PHO knew at the time she
made her decisions. There is no evidence the PHO knew the data she was relying
on at the time was inaccurate.

[
78
]

Finally, the applicant submits that an abuse of
process is made out by evidence of a conspiracy of secrecy involving the PHO,
allegedly aided by various government actors, and ultimately endorsed by this
Court and the Court in
Beaudoin
. As I have already explained, these
attempts to malign the conduct of the PHO ignore a variety of legal and
practical realities that governed her ability to share information freely with
the applicant or other defendants. There is no basis on which to draw the
adverse inferences applicant's counsel urges on the Court.

Conclusion

[
79
]

In conclusion, the burden falls on the applicant
to establish an abuse of process or
Charter
violation on a balance of
probabilities. The applicant has proven there was correspondence about the
gathering and events orders to which the PHO did not respond. Some of these can
rightly be considered requests for reconsideration. The applicant has proven
that for a few days an exemption to the gathering and events order was given by
the Deputy PHO to one group of people to hold a worship service, when the PHO
had just granted a more narrow exemption to the applicant. However, this was
quickly brought into alignment by the PHO.

[
80
]

The applicant has established that a number of local religious
leaders were deeply concerned about the prohibitions on gathering and events,
some of whom challenged and continue to challenge the PHO's authority to make
those orders. The applicant has established that there were people who
struggled and suffered when restrictions on gathering were imposed. It has been
established that some people felt unheard and disagree with the PHO's decision
making. Specifically, there are people who do not believe their worship
gatherings were unsafe, despite the PHO's professional opinion that singing and
prolonged exposure to others indoors could increase risks of infection.

[
81
]

The PHO's decision making has already been
reviewed by the Supreme Court. The applicant has established that there are
people who do not accept that ruling or the ruling of our Court of Appeal that Dr. Henry's
gathering and events orders were a justified infringement of religious
freedoms. None of what has been established amounts to an abuse of process or a
violation of
Charter
rights when it comes to this applicant.

[
82
]

For clarity, what has not been established at this hearing also
includes a number of submissions made by counsel:

1. The
PHO did not prohibit all worship and she did not prohibit worship gatherings
just because they involved worship.

2.
Given the ruling in
Beaudoin
, it cannot be said that the PHO made
gathering and events orders that were unfounded by science and only to bow to
political pressure.

3.
The PHO did not discriminate based on faith in the reconsideration process, nor
did she ignore Christian churches. The PHO did not act with an arrogant
disregard for our right to freely practise religion.

4.
The PHO did not knowingly mislead the courts or otherwise manufacture the
outcome of the precedent‑setting case in
Beaudoin.

And finally,

5. The
careful, detailed legal analysis by a judicially‑independent court in
Beaudoin
is not a
‘rubber‑stamping’ of provincial
law.

[
83
]

The systemic failures alleged by the applicant have not been made
out at this hearing, and any lapses in the reconsideration process have not
impacted this applicant. When Pastor Koopman ultimately made a request for
reconsideration, he was granted an exemption. He sought consultation and
dialogue with the PHO regarding the COVID restrictions before the prohibitions
were imposed, but when this did not occur, he did not initially seek exemptions
to the prohibitions through the s. 43 process.

[
84
]

By this point, Pastor Koopman had decided
engaging with the reconsideration process was tantamount to preferring the
PHO's authority over the word of God. He wanted the PHO to rescind her orders
and back away from interference with the right to worship. The fact that she refused
to do so is not an abuse of process or her power. The Court in
Beaudoin

has already decided the violation of Pastor Koopman’s freedom of religion was
justified. The application for a finding of abuse of process and a stay of
proceedings for his tickets is dismissed.

(ORAL RULING CONCLUDED)
